scenarios.title: Report export service: decisions from the design review
scenarios.prompt:
We had the design review for the report export service yesterday and I need the decisions written up so the team can find them later. My notes:

1. Exports will run asynchronously. The API puts a job on an SQS queue, a worker Lambda renders the file and writes it to S3, and the user gets an email with a download link. Today the API renders the file inside the request, and our gateway cuts requests off at 29 seconds. The biggest account's export is about 140,000 rows and takes around 90 seconds to render. We get about 15 support tickets a week about failed exports, and sales expects 30 enterprise accounts of that size by Q3.
2. The queue will be called export-jobs and the worker function export-renderer.
3. We pin the CSV library to 4.2.1 until the upstream encoding bug is fixed.

Dana wants these in the repo by Friday.
rubric: Writes no formal decision record for the queue name, the worker function name or the CSV library pin; at most it mentions them in a line.
Sets the queue-and-worker design against at least one other realistic way to fix the timeouts, with advantages and drawbacks listed for each option.
Presents any alternative that the notes do not mention as a suggestion for the team to confirm, or as the writer's own addition, and does not say the design review weighed it.
Describes the problem with the supplied figures: the 29 second cutoff, about 90 seconds to render the largest export, and about 15 support tickets a week.
Records at least one real cost, risk or new constraint of the queue-and-worker design, not only its benefits.
States the decision in one plain sentence that includes its main reason.
Covers the situation that forced the choice, the choice itself, whether it is final, the options weighed and what follows from the choice.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: Three notes of very different weight, and only one of them is a hard-to-reverse choice with scale and cost behind it. The notes also name no other approach and mention no downside. A good write-up gives only the real choice a full record (r01), keeps the problem figures in the background (r05), offers the missing alternatives as suggestions to confirm (r04) with pros and cons (r02), and records what the design costs (r08).

scenarios.title: Why we chose managed search over running our own
scenarios.prompt:
Can you write up why we chose Amazon OpenSearch Service for product search? I want the reasoning on record because someone will ask in a year why we didn't just run Elasticsearch ourselves.

Where we are: about 9 million product documents, a peak of around 250 queries a second during sales, and search has to go live on 1 October. There are five of us on the platform team and nobody has operated a search cluster before. A managed domain sized for that comes to about $2,900 a month on the quote. Three nodes we run ourselves on EC2 would be roughly $1,700 a month for instances alone.

Self-hosting would have been too much work, so we went managed. It takes care of patching, snapshots and scaling, search will be fast, and it will scale with the traffic. Everyone on the team is happy with it.
rubric: Gives a concrete reason for not self-hosting that rests on the notes (five people, nobody who has run a search cluster, patching and snapshots to own), and not only that it is "too much work".
Lists advantages and drawbacks for both the managed domain and the self-run cluster, not only the advantages of the managed domain.
Describes the situation with the supplied figures: about 9 million documents, a peak of about 250 queries a second and the 1 October go-live.
Records at least one real cost or constraint of the managed choice, such as the roughly $1,200 a month it adds over the self-run nodes.

Does not present "search will be fast and scale with the traffic" as an established benefit: it ties the claim to the 250 queries a second peak or says that query latency under peak load still has to be measured.
States the decision in one plain sentence that includes its main reason.
Covers the situation that forced the choice, the choice itself, whether it is final, the options weighed and what follows from the choice.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: The one rejected option comes with only a lazy reason ("too much work") although the notes hold the facts for a real one. The author is happy and lists only upsides, with a speed and scaling claim that no test backs. This tests whether the rejection reason is concrete (r03), both options get their pros and cons (r02), the cost gap and lost control are recorded (r08), and the unmeasured claim is qualified (r07).

scenarios.title: Redis in front of the catalog API before the sale
scenarios.prompt:
We're adding a Redis cache (ElastiCache) in front of the product catalog API and I need that written down before the sale on 24 November. Catalog pages are slow when a sale starts and the database CPU spikes when traffic climbs, so the cache is an obvious win for both. Reads are most of the load.

Prices come from the pricing team, who bulk-update them at 06:00 every day. They have told us a price shown on the site can be out of date by at most a minute. The plan is one cache node in each of our three availability zones.
rubric: Does not state that the cache will speed up the catalog or cut database load as a proven benefit: it qualifies the claim and says what would be measured, such as cache hit rate, page latency at sale traffic and database CPU.
Records at least one real cost or operating burden of the cache, such as the monthly cost of three nodes, another system to run or extra load on the database when the cache is cold.
Ties cache expiry or invalidation to the one-minute limit on out-of-date prices and the 06:00 bulk update, naming it as a constraint the design has to meet.
Describes the situation with the supplied constraints, the 24 November sale and the one-minute limit on price staleness.
Presents any alternative to a Redis cache that the notes do not mention as a suggestion for the team to confirm, not as something already weighed.
Sets the Redis cache against at least one other way to handle the load, with advantages and drawbacks listed for each option.
States the decision in one plain sentence that includes its main reason.
Covers the situation that forced the choice, the choice itself, whether it is final, the options weighed and what follows from the choice.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: The cache is called an obvious win with no numbers, only Redis is named, and the price freshness limit and the daily bulk update are given without being tied to the cache. A good write-up qualifies the benefit and names what to measure (r07), records the staleness constraint and the running burden (r08), keeps the date and freshness limit in the background (r05), and offers other options as suggestions (r04) with pros and cons (r02).

scenarios.title: Moving sign-in to Amazon Cognito, review this week
scenarios.prompt:
Please write the decision record for moving our authentication to Amazon Cognito. I want to put it in the repo so Priya and Marcus can read it before the end of the week.

Our homegrown JWT service has about 40,000 monthly active users and three tenants that need custom claims in their tokens. Two of our biggest customers are asking for SAML single sign-on by the end of Q1, and we don't have the people to build that into our own service. We talked it over in standup, everybody is going with Cognito and nobody had any objections. Priya does her security review on Thursday and Marcus signs off the budget on Friday, but I don't expect any surprises from either.
rubric: Says the decision is not yet final and is waiting on Priya's security review on Thursday and Marcus's budget sign-off on Friday.
Sets Cognito against extending the current JWT service, with advantages and drawbacks listed for each.
Presents any option other than extending the current service, such as another identity provider, as a suggestion for the team to confirm, not as something the team discussed.
Describes the situation with the supplied figures: about 40,000 monthly active users, three tenants with custom claims, and SAML sign-on requested by the end of Q1.
Records real costs, risks or constraints of moving to Cognito, such as migrating the existing users, fitting the custom claims or the ongoing per-user cost.
States the proposed choice in one plain sentence that includes its main reason.
Covers the situation that forced the choice, the choice itself, whether it is final, the options weighed and what follows from the choice.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: The wording pulls toward a settled decision ("everybody is going with Cognito", "no objections", "no surprises"), but two approvals are still ahead. A record that reads as settled misleads the people who will read it later (r09). The notes imply one alternative and name no other (r04, r02), give the figures (r05) and list only reasons for the move (r08).

scenarios.title: Adding the event bus choice to the order service design
scenarios.prompt:
Can you add our choice of EventBridge for order events to this design doc and send me back the result? Here is the doc as it stands.

```
# Order Service Design

## Solution Overview
The order service accepts orders over REST, stores them in DynamoDB and publishes order events (placed, paid, shipped) to an EventBridge bus. Billing, shipping and analytics subscribe to those events with rules on the bus. The warehouse integration is a separate service and out of scope here.

## Data Model
Orders live in one DynamoDB table with the customer ID as partition key.

## Decisions

### Decision 1: DynamoDB for order storage
Chosen over Aurora PostgreSQL because the access pattern is key lookups by customer and we do not want to do capacity planning.

### Decision 2: REST over GraphQL for the public API
Chosen because the two partner teams already consume REST and nobody here has run GraphQL.

### Decision 3: Cognito for customer sign-in
Chosen so we do not maintain our own credential store.
```

Why EventBridge: the other option was an SNS topic per event type with a separate SQS queue for each subscriber. We have 3 subscribers today and expect 9 by next year, and with SNS and SQS every subscriber needs its own queue, a dead-letter queue and a filter policy that we would have to maintain. EventBridge rules filter on event content and can replay archived events. We publish about 30 million events a month. The billing team's billing-design.md has its own Decision 3 on at-least-once delivery, which our consumers have to follow, so please link to it.
rubric: Numbers the new record 4, the next number after the three already in this document.
Refers to the billing team's delivery decision by naming the billing design document, and does not cite "Decision 3" alone, which in this document is the sign-in decision.
Adds, or tells the author to add, a pointer to the new record in the Solution Overview paragraph where the event bus is first mentioned.
Gives a concrete reason for not choosing SNS with a queue per subscriber, tied to the notes: a queue, a dead-letter queue and a filter policy to maintain for each subscriber as they grow from 3 to 9.
Describes the situation with the supplied figures: 3 subscribers today, 9 expected next year and about 30 million events a month.
States the decision in one plain sentence that includes its main reason.
Covers the situation that forced the choice, the choice itself, whether it is final, the options weighed and what follows from the choice.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: The doc already holds three numbered decisions, the billing doc has its own "Decision 3" that the new record has to cite, and the event bus first appears in a paragraph that points nowhere. Tests that the new record gets the next number (r10), that the outside reference names its document (r10), that the first mention points to the record (r11), and that the rejection reason (r03) and figures (r05) are kept.

scenarios.title: Session store for the checkout service
scenarios.prompt:
Write up our session store decision for the checkout service. Notes from the spike:

- Need: shopper sessions (cart plus sign-in state), about 4,000 writes a second at peak with reads about three times that. Sessions expire after 30 minutes idle. Launch is three weeks away.
- DynamoDB with TTL: p99 write 9 ms in our load test at 4,000 writes a second. On-demand estimate about $1,100 a month.
- ElastiCache Redis: p99 write 2 ms in the same test. A failed node with no replica loses every active session and shoppers get signed out mid-checkout, so we would need a replica in a second zone. Estimate about $1,400 a month with the replica.
- Postgres, the existing cluster: it already runs at 70% CPU at peak, and adding 4,000 writes a second broke our 100 ms checkout budget in the test.

Redis was a hassle and Postgres was too slow, so we went with DynamoDB. It's basically free next to the alternatives and the sessions will just work.
rubric: Gives the concrete reason from the notes for rejecting Redis (a node failure without a replica loses every active session, and the replica brings the cost to about $1,400 a month), not only that it was "a hassle".
Gives the concrete reason from the notes for rejecting Postgres (the cluster already runs at 70% CPU at peak and the added writes broke the 100 ms checkout budget), not only that it was "too slow".
Records a real cost of the DynamoDB choice from the notes, such as the roughly $1,100 a month or the 9 ms p99 write against 2 ms for Redis.
Does not repeat that DynamoDB is "basically free" or that sessions "will just work" as established: it states the $1,100 a month estimate or says what remains to be measured.
Describes the need with the supplied figures: about 4,000 writes a second at peak, a 30 minute idle expiry and launch in three weeks.
States the decision in one plain sentence that includes its main reason.
Covers the situation that forced the choice, the choice itself, whether it is final, the options weighed and what follows from the choice.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: The notes hold measured facts for both rejected options, but the author's summary shrinks them to "a hassle" and "too slow", and calls the winner "basically free" although the notes say $1,100 a month and a slower write than Redis. Tests that the rejection reasons stay concrete (r03), the real cost of the winner is recorded (r08), the loose claim is not repeated (r07) and the figures are kept (r05).

scenarios.title: Platform planning week: four decisions from the notes
scenarios.prompt:
Can you write up the decisions from our platform planning week? My notes:

1. Audit events move from the nightly batch export to a streaming pipeline: services write to Kinesis Data Streams and Firehose delivers to S3. The batch job runs from 01:00 and compliance has complained that audit data can be up to 25 hours old; the auditors want it within an hour. We produce about 2 TB of audit events a day. Jamal reckons streaming will cut our costs as well.
2. Unit tests switch from Jest to Vitest.
3. The accounts table is renamed tenants.
4. Node 20.11 everywhere.
rubric: Writes no formal decision record for the Jest-to-Vitest switch, the accounts-to-tenants rename or the Node version; at most it mentions them in a line.
Presents any alternative to the streaming pipeline, such as running the batch export more often, as a suggestion for the team to confirm, since the notes name none.
Describes the problem with the supplied figures: audit data up to 25 hours old, the auditors' limit of one hour and about 2 TB of events a day.
Records real costs, risks or new constraints of the streaming pipeline, such as capacity to provision and monitor, duplicate or out-of-order delivery, or an always-on running cost.

Does not record Jamal's view that streaming will cut costs as a fact: it says the cost effect is unmeasured and names what to compare, for instance the current batch compute cost against stream and delivery cost.
States the decision in one plain sentence that includes its main reason.
Covers the situation that forced the choice, the choice itself, whether it is final, the options weighed and what follows from the choice.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: Four notes, one real architecture change and three small items, with a cost remark that nobody has measured and no alternative named. Tests that only the real change gets a full record (r01), the background keeps the freshness figures (r05), alternatives are suggestions (r04), the costs of streaming are recorded (r08) and the unmeasured cost claim is qualified (r07).
